text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Swedish households have a pessimistic view of 1997, with only 21.5 percent believing the economy will improve, a survey by official statistics bureau Statistics Sweden shows.

- Volvo continues to introduce new cars at a quick tempo, the latest its C70 cabriolet unveiled at a car show in Detroit, U.S.. Volvo expects to sell at least half the luxury cars in the U.S. and also is targeting European and Japanese markets.
- Thieves break into over 1,000 residences in central Stockholm each year.

- Sales of Volvo in Britian rose 35 percent in December compared to a year ago, giving a fall for the year of 15 percent. Saab sales rose 22 percent in December versus December 1995 and 29 percent in 1996 compared to 1995.
- The Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development says unemployment and wage structure are the biggest weaknesses in the Swedish economy.

- Global telecommunications firm LM Ericsson AB won a court case in which it refused to produce certain documents for tax authorities because the documents were considered top secret. The case may set a precedent.

- Several unions will demand shortening working hours by between 16 and 25 hours per year in the coming round of wage negotiations, part of a larger goal of the unions to reduce the working year by 100 hours.
- Volvo's first cabriolet since the 1950s, the C70, will be targeting a luxury market in the U.S. where 40,000 cars are sold per year. Its main competitiors will be BMW and Mercedes-Benz.
- Viewers could see television for the first time in Sweden on the Internet for a short time on Tuesday.

- Swedish subway operator SL would like to reduce the number of suicides on the tracks, possibly by installing television cameras. There are some 10 deaths estimated each year on the Stockholm underground lines.

- Swedish investors, rushing to avoid a tax hike on capital gains from the sale of a certain type of mutual fund, took their money and ran in December. Investors in the year's final month have removed over seven billion crowns from the Swedish mututal funds known as "allemansfonder".

- Sweden's banks will not be allowed to establish a joint data base to keep track of people it suspects of money laundering. A county court in Stockholm has upheld a previous ruling by a governemnt agency which suggested that the right to personal privacy has precedence over the bank's battle against illegal money laundering.

- The Swedish government has been forced to delay by a half-year its planned increase of the tax on industries which emit carbon dioxide into the environment. The energy tax was to be doubled starting on January but it now looks like industry will have a lengthy respite.
- Volvo hopes to boost profits and spice up its image with the latest addition to the Volve family - the C70 convertible - which was presented at a car show in Detroit on Tuesday.
